title: The Duck with a Blue Bill That Almost Disappeared—and Came Back!
summary:
Have you ever seen a duck with a bright blue bill? The white-headed duck is one of the weirdest ducks in the world! Its name comes from its white head, but the coolest part is the male's sky-blue bill. And that's not all—they have long, stiff tail feathers that stick up like a whisk broom. They're so unusual that one expert called them "one of the true eccentrics of the waterfowl world."

In spring, male white-headed ducks put on an amazing show to attract females. They swim sideways, splash water, and beat their puffed-up neck feathers with their bills to make bubble trails. Their tail feathers wave like flags and slap the water like paddles. "To witness white-headed ducks in courtship is to watch one of the avian world's most extraordinary performances," says expert Nicky Petkov.

But these ducks have a serious story too. In the past, people drained their wetland homes for farms and buildings, and hunters shot them. By the late 1970s, only 22 white-headed ducks were left in all of Spain! That's fewer than a classroom of kids. So Spain started a big effort to protect wetlands and ban hunting. Now, Spain has about 2,500 white-headed ducks. That's a huge comeback!

But the story isn't over. Globally, the species is still endangered. And there's a new threat: ruddy ducks. These are an invasive species (animals that come from somewhere else and cause problems) that escaped from a wildlife reserve in Britain. They spread to Spain and started competing with white-headed ducks for mates. They even made babies with them, which could make white-headed ducks disappear genetically. In Western Europe, people have been removing ruddy ducks to help, but the risk is still there.

Climate change and droughts also threaten wetlands. So the white-headed duck's future depends on protecting wetlands everywhere. As Petkov says, "The story is not finished." But it's a great example of how people can help save a species!
why_it_matters: This story shows that when people take care of nature, animals can recover, and it also reminds us that new problems like invasive species can put that recovery at risk.

background_read: The white-headed duck lives in shallow wetlands, which are being drained in many parts of the world for farms and cities, and Spain (a country in southwestern Europe) is one of its most important homes.
Ruddy ducks are native to North America; some escaped from a wildlife reserve in Britain, another European country, and reached Spain, where they compete with white-headed ducks.
Removing an invasive species is hard work, but this story shows that protecting habitats and removing newcomers can help native animals recover.
Article_Structure: WHO: Bird experts like Nicky Petkov and conservationists in Spain.
WHAT: The white-headed duck came back from just 22 birds in Spain to about 2,500 after people protected wetlands and banned hunting, but it is still endangered.
WHERE: Wetlands in Spain and other parts of Western Europe.
WHY: Draining wetlands, hunting, invasive ruddy ducks, and climate change threaten the species, so saving it depends on protecting wetland habitats.

perspectives.description: They see the duck's comeback as proof that saving wetlands and stopping hunting works.
They worry that ruddy ducks and drought could undo the gains, so they keep working to remove the invaders.
They call the duck an eccentric species whose future is still far from certain.
